meta.provenance_line: District revenue positions are modeled from commuter, visitor and character multipliers against the city baseline.

myth.claim: The highest-revenue district is the best place to open.
myth.strike_label: the loudest is the best place
myth.reality: It is the highest-revenue district. It is also the one the lease punishes hardest. Top takings come with the heaviest rent, so the lift is spent before it reaches the till. On rent, the loudest names sit heaviest and a few quieter districts run far lighter.
myth.stat_label: rent runs well above the city rate
myth.tell: The best-known address is the one the lease punishes hardest.

districts.name: Mayfair
districts.blurb: The highest takings in the city, paid for with the highest rent. A trade only clears here if its ticket is large enough to swallow the lease.
districts.verdict: Highest takings, heaviest lease. Worth it only for a large-ticket trade that can carry the rent.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: Expense-account lunches and dinners carry an average ticket no suburb matches.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: Office workers and visitors drive steady morning and mid-afternoon peaks.

best_trades.name: Salon
best_trades.why: A wealthy resident and worker base pays full price for regular upkeep.

locals_know: The Bond Street rent is for the postcode; the streets behind it, Bruton and Bourdon, carry the same address at roughly a third of the headline lease.
Trade is weekday and lunch led; expense-account tables thin out after 3pm and the whole quarter empties on Sundays.
Ground-floor frontage here is priced for flagship retail, so a service trade does better one floor up at a fraction of the rate.
August is dead: the international residents who carry spend are out of town, and a fixed-rent unit still has to be paid through it.

districts.name: Covent Garden
districts.blurb: Visitor footfall does the heavy lifting. Volume is enormous but it skews to one-time customers, so loyalty is hard to build.
districts.verdict: Enormous visitor volume, almost no repeat custom. The margin lives entirely in the first sale.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: Constant visitor churn keeps seats turning over all day.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: A captive crowd between attractions eats close to where it stands.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: Pre and post-theatre trade fills the evening hours.

locals_know: The Piazza itself is managed frontage with a premium above the streets around it; Neal Street and Monmouth Street carry the same crowd for materially less.
The crowd is transient, so a loyalty scheme earns almost nothing here; price the first visit as if it is the only one.
Evenings ride the theatre turnover, not a lunch-to-dinner build, so the kitchen has to peak twice, not once.

districts.name: Soho
districts.blurb: An evening economy. Days are quiet, nights are dense, and a trade either lives off the after-dark crowd or struggles.
districts.verdict: A night economy on a daytime lease. The evening crowd has to pay for the hours the unit sits quiet.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: A dense, late-running evening crowd anchors the district.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: Pre and post-night dining packs tables into a few hours.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: Media offices want fast coffee through the working day.

locals_know: A late licence is the real moat here, harder to win and worth more than the lease; a unit that already holds one to 3am trades at a premium for good reason.
Daytime rent is paid by night-time takings, so a lunch offer that only breaks even is still worth running to hold the frontage.
The media crowd anchors weekday evenings and the tourists carry the weekend, two different rooms that want two different menus.
Delivery kitchens have quietly taken the back units off Wardour Street, so street-level rent is now competing with a cheaper dark-kitchen model next door.

districts.name: Canary Wharf
districts.blurb: A weekday office island. Footfall is huge Monday to Friday at lunch and collapses on weekends, so the model has to win in five days.
districts.verdict: Five days of dense office lunch, then nothing. The whole year of rent is earned before the weekend.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: The morning commute and mid-afternoon breaks drive two reliable peaks.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: Tens of thousands need a fast lunch in a short midday window.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: An after-work crowd unwinds on site before the long commute home.

locals_know: The estate is privately managed, so the lease often comes with mall-style service charges and trading hours on top of the headline rent.
Weekends are effectively dead; a seven-day cost base has to be earned in five, which is why throughput beats ambience every time.
The lunch rush is narrow and violent, roughly 12 to 1:30; a queue that moves slowly loses the whole day's margin.
Hybrid working thinned Mondays and Fridays first, so the reliable week is now really three days, not five.

districts.name: Shoreditch
districts.blurb: A creative and tech crowd with money and taste. Rent is climbing but still leaves room for an independent operator to clear a margin.
districts.verdict: Money and taste, and rent that still leaves room, for now. Sign early or watch the margin close.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: A tech and freelance crowd treats cafes as a second office.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: A young, spending crowd eats out often and tries new openings.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: A strong evening scene runs on a still-moderate lease.

locals_know: Rent is still rising fast on the prime blocks; a lease signed today at today's rate can look heavy inside two years, so a rent review clause matters more than the opening figure.
Redchurch Street commands a designer-retail premium, but a unit one block onto Cheshire Street or Club Row carries the same crowd for noticeably less.
The customer splits in two: weekday tech offices want fast coffee and lunch, weekend market crowds want to browse, and few units serve both well.

districts.name: Camden
districts.blurb: Market-led footfall, heavy on weekends and light on spend per head. Volume is real but the average ticket is modest.
districts.verdict: Huge weekend volume at a small ticket. The model is throughput, not spend per head.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: Weekend market crowds graze across the day.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: A built-in music scene fills the evenings.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: High weekend volume on a modest average ticket.

locals_know: A stall inside the market trades on a licence and a turnover cut rather than a full lease, which is how a food trader tests the crowd here before committing to a unit.
Spend per head is genuinely low; the model only works on volume, so a slow till or a small kitchen caps the whole business.
The weekend carries the week, which means the weekday fixed cost is the real risk, not the Saturday queue.

districts.name: Hackney
districts.blurb: A residential creative belt that spends locally. Trade is steady and loyal rather than spiky, and rent stays reasonable for now.
districts.verdict: Steady, loyal, local spend on a light lease. Slower to fill than the centre, but it holds.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: A resident creative crowd treats the local cafe as a daily habit.

best_trades.name: Grocery
best_trades.why: Households shop locally and value quality over price.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: Loyal local diners hold up better than a spiky destination crowd.

locals_know: Loyalty is the real asset here; a good local builds a base that carries it through a downturn better than any footfall district.
Broadway Market rent is set by the Saturday crowd, but a unit on Chatsworth Road or Lower Clapton serves the same residents at a weekday-rent rate.
Trade leans residential, so it actually holds up on weekends when the centre empties, the opposite of the office districts.
The catchment walks or cycles in, so a delivery-heavy model wastes the one thing this district gives you, which is a base that comes back in person.

districts.name: Stratford
districts.blurb: A transit and shopping-centre crowd passing through. Footfall is high but mall economics and chain competition cap what an independent can take.
districts.verdict: High footfall on a cheap lease, but the mall sets the terms. Independents win on speed, not range.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: A constant flow of people moving between train and mall.

best_trades.name: Grocery
best_trades.why: Commuters and new-build residents grab everyday essentials nearby.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: A large residential catchment eats out close to home.

locals_know: There are two rent worlds here: inside Westfield you pay mall rates with mall rules, and on the older Broadway you pay a fraction for a rougher, slower crowd.
The mall sets the trading hours and the tenant mix, so an independent competes on convenience and speed, never on range against the chains.
The footfall is high but rushed; people are moving between train and shops, so impulse and grab-and-go beat anything that asks them to sit and browse.

districts.name: Brixton
districts.blurb: South of the river, below the city baseline on revenue, but on one of the lightest leases on the map.
districts.verdict: Below the city on takings, on one of the lightest leases of the districts here.

best_trades.name: Restaurant
best_trades.why: A food-led crowd rewards a distinctive independent kitchen.

best_trades.name: Bar
best_trades.why: A strong evening economy runs on a lighter lease than the centre.

best_trades.name: Cafe
best_trades.why: Residents by day and visitors at the weekend both anchor trade.

locals_know: Revenue sits below the city, but the rent is among the lightest on the map, which is the whole reason operators look here.
A stall in Brixton Village is cheaper than a street unit and just as visible to the food crowd, so it is where most kitchens here start.
The evening economy is strong and cheaper to run than the centre, so a bar clears here on volume the West End would need a much bigger ticket to match.
The market draws from across London at weekends but the weekday trade is local, so a menu that only works on the destination crowd will feel Tuesdays hard.
